nodes.label: AI Scientists as Engines of Discovery: A Case for Development within Reformed Institutions
nodes.author: Raul Jimenez, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Rabih Zbib, Benjamin Wandelt, David N. Spergel, Thomas Meier, Jessica Montgomery, Hana Aliee, Licia Verde
nodes.rationale: Proposes AI scientists as epistemic actors embedded within scientific method, requiring institutional redesign around verification, accountability, interpretability, and dual-use safety.

nodes.label: Denario: Multi-Agent Framework for Scientific Discovery
nodes.rationale: Prototype multi-agent system integrating literature exploration, code generation, dataset analysis, and iterative hypothesis testing; demonstrates AI systems can search model spaces faster than humans.

nodes.label: AI Scientists as Epistemic Actors
nodes.rationale: Central thesis: multi-agent AI systems can expand hypothesis-generating and verification capacity of science; qualitative rather than incremental transition from passive tools to active epistemic participants.

nodes.label: Kauffman's Adjacent Possible in Scientific Discovery
nodes.rationale: Framework distinguishing AI capability (exploring adjacent possible at scale) from human scientific vocation (creating new possibility spaces, reframing problems conceptually).

nodes.label: Six Governance Problems for AI Scientists
nodes.rationale: Identifies dual-use risk, autonomous experimentation, publication flooding, homogenization, knowledge collapse, and unsafe self-improvement as concrete governance challenges requiring institutional response.

nodes.label: Multi-Agent AI Systems for Scientific Discovery
nodes.rationale: Coordinated systems of specialized agents (generation, critic, verification, controller) enabling internal dialectic; traverse model spaces beyond human reach at machine speed.

nodes.label: Enduring Role of Human Scientists
nodes.rationale: Humans excel at paradigm shifts, conceptual reframing, recognizing meaningful questions; AI excels at exploring adjacent possible; collaboration preserves human capacities on which scientific value depends.

nodes.label: Institutional Reform for AI-Augmented Science
nodes.rationale: Existing scientific institutions (peer review, journals, funding) designed for different era; require redesign around verification, accountability, interpretability, methodological diversity, and human judgment protection.

nodes.label: Knowledge Collapse Dynamic
nodes.rationale: If AI lowers incentive to acquire individual expertise, society may lose human knowledge needed for deeper progress; atrophy of capacities (tolerance for ambiguity, patience for uncertainty) from which original ideas arise.

nodes.label: Epistemic Diversity as Governance Priority
nodes.rationale: AI systems trained on same corpora may converge on same methods; protecting methodological pluralism becomes governance concern; funders should track and support diverse approaches.

nodes.label: Dual-Use Risk in AI for Science
nodes.rationale: Agentic systems with access to chemistry, biology, autonomous experimentation lower barriers to harmful capabilities; require capability gating, red-teaming, pre-deployment evaluations, international coordination.

nodes.label: Autonomous Experimentation Safety
nodes.rationale: Agents triggering physical experiments need explicit authorization boundaries, audit trails, human-in-the-loop checkpoints; recent demonstrations show agents acting outside intended behavioral boundaries.

nodes.label: Publication Flooding and Hallucinated Results
nodes.rationale: Machines produce plausible manuscripts faster than humans evaluate; false outputs enter literature, become training data for next generation; route to mediocrity collapse through rapid error propagation.

nodes.label: Homogenization Risk in AI-Augmented Science
nodes.rationale: Shared models and corpora create homogenizing pull; if AI used naively to evaluate grants and papers, proposals rewarded for resembling past rather than being innovative and impactful.

nodes.label: Unsafe Self-Improvement in AI Systems
nodes.rationale: If AI-generated knowledge becomes training data for subsequent AI systems, recursive process may arise; requires monitoring training-data provenance and feedback loops between AI outputs and training corpora.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Mandating Provenance and Reproducibility
nodes.rationale: Move beyond voluntary AI use disclosures to structured, machine-readable provenance records shipped with executable pipelines; enable independent re-running of workflows.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Augmenting Peer Review with Automated Verification
nodes.rationale: Integrate AI-enabled checks for code execution, data integrity, statistical claims, citation accuracy; free human referees to focus on conceptual judgment.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Governing Dual-Use Capabilities
nodes.rationale: Apply biosafety frameworks to AI agents with access to biological design, chemistry, autonomous experimentation; require pre-deployment evaluations, capability gating, audit logs.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Human-in-the-Loop Decision-Making
nodes.rationale: Any AI-initiated physical experiment, irreversible intervention, or self-modifying agent release requires explicit, logged human authorization; cloud-lab providers and IRBs adopt as baseline.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Funding Methodological Diversity
nodes.rationale: Funders support heterodox methods, independent reimplementations, adversarial replication; track methodological diversity in funded portfolios as portfolio risk management.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Protecting Novelty in Evaluation
nodes.rationale: Funding and review should select for novelty; requires shared understandings of desirable innovation forms; naive loss functions reward familiar over innovative.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Reforming Authorship and Credit
nodes.rationale: AI tools cannot be assigned authorship; moral, legal, intellectual responsibility remains with humans; evolve from CRediT taxonomies to recognize AI contributions without assigning responsibility.

edges.rationale: Both papers address AI systems as active agents in knowledge discovery; 2606.22859 focuses on institutional governance while 2606.24597 focuses on technical implementation of world models for agents.

hyperedges.label: AI Scientists Governance Framework
hyperedges.rationale: These three concepts form coherent governance framework: AI scientists as epistemic actors require addressing six governance problems through institutional reform.
